title: Growing radish microgreens
subtitle: Fast brassica cotyledons in 5 to 7 days on a windowsill or countertop
excerpt: Radish microgreens are one of the quickest crops you can grow indoors. Sow densely on a 25 cm tray, blackout for two days, move to light, and cut with scissors at the cotyledon stage in 5 to 7 days. The cotyledons are peppery and crisp.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) indoor growing pages. Standard microgreen-growing practice as synthesised from extension service material and widely-taught tray methods.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

content.text: Radish microgreens are a year-round indoor crop sown in a 25 cm tray on a countertop or windowsill. The sowing-to-cut arc is 5 to 7 days: sow, cover and blackout for two days to push up straight stems, bring into light, cut with kitchen scissors when the cotyledons open. The cotyledons have a clean, sharp peppery bite that is stronger than a full-grown radish.

Radish is the standard starting point for first-time microgreen growers because it is fast, tolerates a range of conditions, and gives immediate feedback. If anything goes wrong in the tray, the short cycle means you can adjust and try again within the same week.

Light source: a south-facing or west-facing windowsill works in summer. In winter, natural light is borderline; an LED grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours a day gives taller, more uniform cotyledons than a dim window.

Ambient temperature: 18 to 22°C is the sweet spot. Radish germinates and grows faster than most microgreen crops and is not especially temperature-sensitive, but cold rooms (below 15°C) slow the cycle noticeably. A kitchen counter away from cold draughts is a reliable position.

Day 0: sow. Fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim with pre-dampened seed compost or coir. Level and press lightly. Scatter radish seed densely across the surface, about 20 to 30 g per 25 cm tray. Press seeds gently into contact with the medium but do not cover with soil. Radish microgreen seed is small enough to lie on the surface and germinate without burial.

Days 1 to 2: blackout. Stack a second empty tray on top of the sown tray, weighted with something flat (a book, a second sown tray). The weight and darkness cause the shoots to push straight upward. Check the tray once daily; the seeds germinate quickly and sprout into the underside of the covering tray within 36 to 48 hours.

Day 3 onward: light. Remove the cover once the shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall and standing upright. Move to light. The cotyledons green up rapidly (usually within 24 hours of their first light exposure). Water from below: set the growing tray inside a second tray, add a centimetre of water, and let the growing medium draw it up.
keeps the surface dry and dramatically reduces mould risk.

Days 5 to 7: cut. Radish cotyledons are ready when they have expanded fully and stand 5 to 8 cm tall. The first true leaves may just be showing; cut before they develop further, as the cotyledon stage has the best flavour and texture. Hold the stems near the base and cut with sharp scissors 1 cm above the growing medium. Rinse, spin dry, use fresh or refrigerate in a sealed container for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting the tray
attrs.intro: Five common problems in radish microgreen trays and what they mean.

items.symptom: Stems collapse and rot at the base, cotyledons go dark and wet
items.cause: Damping off, usually from overwatering or poor airflow.
items.fix: Switch to bottom watering only. Do not top-water seedlings at any stage. Improve airflow around the tray. Start a fresh tray; damping off spreads and the affected tray is lost.

items.symptom: White fuzzy growth on the growing medium between the stems
items.cause: Mould on the medium surface, from surface moisture or poor ventilation.
items.fix: This is surface mould on the substrate, not on the seedlings, and is usually safe to eat around. Increase airflow (a small fan nearby helps). Bottom water only. The mould resolves as the cotyledons grow and shade the surface.

items.symptom: Uneven germination across the tray, bare patches
items.cause: Uneven seed distribution, dry edges, or cool spots near the tray rim.
items.fix: Scatter seed more evenly next time (a pinch-and-drag motion covers the surface more evenly than a dump-and-spread). Make sure the tray sits on a flat, warm surface. The edges of a tray on a cold windowsill in winter dry out faster than the centre.

items.symptom: Stems are tall and pale, cotyledons small and limp
items.cause: Insufficient light after the blackout phase, or blackout kept on too long.
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Remove the blackout cover as soon as shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall; leaving it longer produces etiolated stems.

items.symptom: Cotyledons taste very bitter or have an unpleasant aftertaste
items.cause: Harvest too late; first true leaves forming and the flavour compounds change.
items.fix: Cut earlier, at the fully-expanded cotyledon stage before true leaves appear. Radish flavour peaks at the cotyledon stage and becomes more pungent and harsh as the plant matures.

content.text: Use untreated, microgreen-grade radish seed. Standard vegetable radish seed often carries a fungicide coating (thiram) to protect field crops; this is not suitable for consumption at the cotyledon stage. Microgreen suppliers sell untreated seed in larger packs at a lower per-gram cost.

is the main risk with microgreen growing, not a pest or a cultural issue. The short cycle of radish microgreens means a failed tray is a low-cost lesson, and the fast turnaround (a fresh tray ready in 5 to 7 days) makes iteration quick.

After cutting, the spent tray with its roots and medium can go directly to the compost. Rinse the plastic tray with hot water and mild washing-up liquid, dry fully, and it is ready for the next cycle. Reusing a tray without cleaning it introduces mould spores from the previous cycle and raises the risk of problems in the next batch.
